  have h1 : ¬ q.1 < q.2 := by omega
  have h2 : ¬ q.1 = q.2 := by omega
  simp [iPiece, h1, h2]

lemma mem_sSub_of_lt {n m : ℤ} (h : n < m) {a : A} (ha : a ∈ 𝒜 (n, wt m)) : a ∈ sSub D wt := by
  refine le_iSup (sPiece D wt) (n, m) ?_
  simpa [sPiece, h] using ha

lemma mem_sSub_of_diag {m : ℤ} {a : A} (ha : a ∈ 𝒜 (m, wt m)) (hd : D.d a = 0) :
    a ∈ sSub D wt := by
  refine le_iSup (sPiece D wt) (m, m) ?_
  simp only [sPiece, lt_irrefl, if_false]
  exact ⟨ha, by simpa using hd⟩

lemma mem_sIdeal_of_lt {n m : ℤ} (h : n < m) {a : A} (ha : a ∈ 𝒜 (n, wt m)) :
    a ∈ sIdeal D wt := by
  refine le_iSup (iPiece D wt) (n, m) ?_
  simpa [iPiece, h] using ha

lemma mem_sIdeal_of_diag {m : ℤ} {c : A} (hc : c ∈ 𝒜 (m - 1, wt m)) :
    D.d c ∈ sIdeal D wt := by
  refine le_iSup (iPiece D wt) (m, m) ?_
  simp only [iPiece, lt_irrefl, if_false]
  exact ⟨c, hc, rfl⟩

/-! ### Multiplicative structure -/

lemma sPiece_mul_le (q q' : ℤ × ℤ) : sPiece D wt q * sPiece D wt q' ≤ sSub D wt := by
  refine Submodule.mul_le.mpr fun a ha b hb => ?_
  have hgi : a ∈ 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) := sPiece_le_graded D wt q ha
  have hgj : b ∈ 𝒜 (q'.1, wt q'.2) := sPiece_le_graded D wt q' hb
  have hab : a * b ∈ 𝒜 (q.1 + q'.1, wt (q.2 + q'.2)) := by
    have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hgi hgj
    simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add] using this
  rcases lt_trichotomy q.1 q.2 with h1 | h1 | h1
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sSub_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · exact mem_sSub_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sSub_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · have hda : D.d a = 0 := by
        have hne : ¬ q.1 < q.2 := by omega
        simp only [sPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h1] at ha
        simpa using ha.2
      have hdb : D.d b = 0 := by
        have hne : ¬ q'.1 < q'.2 := by omega
        simp only [sPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h2] at hb
        simpa using hb.2
      have heq : q.1 + q'.1 = q.2 + q'.2 := by omega
      refine mem_sSub_of_diag D wt (m := q.2 + q'.2) (by rwa [heq] at hab) ?_
      rw [D.leibniz q.1 (wt q.2) a b hgi, hda, hdb]
      simp
    · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h1] at ha; simp at ha; simp [ha]

lemma sSub_mul_mem {a b : A} (ha : a ∈ sSub D wt) (hb : b ∈ sSub D wt) :
    a * b ∈ sSub D wt := by
  have hle : sSub D wt * sSub D wt ≤ sSub D wt := by
    unfold sSub
    rw [Submodule.iSup_mul]
    refine iSup_le fun q => ?_
    rw [Submodule.mul_iSup]
    exact iSup_le fun q' => sPiece_mul_le D wt q q'
  exact hle (Submodule.mul_mem_mul ha hb)

lemma one_mem_sSub : (1 : A) ∈ sSub D wt := by
  have h1 : (1 : A) ∈ 𝒜 ((0 : ℤ), wt 0) := by simpa using SetLike.one_mem_graded 𝒜
  exact mem_sSub_of_diag D wt (m := 0) h1 D.d_one

lemma iPiece_mul_le (q q' : ℤ × ℤ) : iPiece D wt q * sPiece D wt q' ≤ sIdeal D wt := by
  refine Submodule.mul_le.mpr fun a ha b hb => ?_
  have hgi : a ∈ 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) := iPiece_le_graded D wt q ha
  have hgj : b ∈ 𝒜 (q'.1, wt q'.2) := sPiece_le_graded D wt q' hb
  have hab : a * b ∈ 𝒜 (q.1 + q'.1, wt (q.2 + q'.2)) := by
    have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hgi hgj
    simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add] using this
  rcases lt_trichotomy q.1 q.2 with h1 | h1 | h1
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · obtain ⟨c, hc, rfl⟩ : ∃ c ∈ 𝒜 (q.1 - 1, wt q.2), D.d c = a := by
        have hne : ¬ q.1 < q.2 := by omega
        simp only [iPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h1] at ha
        obtain ⟨c, hc, hcc⟩ := ha
        exact ⟨c, hc, hcc⟩
      have hdb : D.d b = 0 := by
        have hne : ¬ q'.1 < q'.2 := by omega
        simp only [sPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h2] at hb
        simpa using hb.2
      have hcb : c * b ∈ 𝒜 (q.2 + q'.2 - 1, wt (q.2 + q'.2)) := by
        have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hc hgj
        simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add,
          show q.1 - 1 + q'.1 = q.2 + q'.2 - 1 from by omega] using this
      have hkey : D.d c * b = D.d (c * b) := by
        rw [D.leibniz (q.1 - 1) (wt q.2) c b hc, hdb]
        simp
      rw [hkey]
      exact mem_sIdeal_of_diag D wt hcb
    · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rw [iPiece_eq_bot D wt h1] at ha; simp at ha; simp [ha]

lemma mul_iPiece_le (q q' : ℤ × ℤ) : sPiece D wt q * iPiece D wt q' ≤ sIdeal D wt := by
  refine Submodule.mul_le.mpr fun a ha b hb => ?_
  have hgi : a ∈ 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) := sPiece_le_graded D wt q ha
  have hgj : b ∈ 𝒜 (q'.1, wt q'.2) := iPiece_le_graded D wt q' hb
  have hab : a * b ∈ 𝒜 (q.1 + q'.1, wt (q.2 + q'.2)) := by
    have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hgi hgj
    simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add] using this
  rcases lt_trichotomy q.1 q.2 with h1 | h1 | h1
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · rw [iPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rcases lt_trichotomy q'.1 q'.2 with h2 | h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (by omega) hab
    · obtain ⟨c, hc, rfl⟩ : ∃ c ∈ 𝒜 (q'.1 - 1, wt q'.2), D.d c = b := by
        have hne : ¬ q'.1 < q'.2 := by omega
        simp only [iPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h2] at hb
        obtain ⟨c, hc, hcc⟩ := hb
        exact ⟨c, hc, hcc⟩
      have hda : D.d a = 0 := by
        have hne : ¬ q.1 < q.2 := by omega
        simp only [sPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h1] at ha
        simpa using ha.2
      have hac : a * c ∈ 𝒜 (q.2 + q'.2 - 1, wt (q.2 + q'.2)) := by
        have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hgi hc
        simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add,
          show q.1 + (q'.1 - 1) = q.2 + q'.2 - 1 from by omega] using this
      have hkey : a * D.d c = (D.sgn q.1)⁻¹ • D.d (a * c) := by
        rw [D.leibniz q.1 (wt q.2) a c hgi, hda, zero_mul, zero_add, smul_smul,
          inv_mul_cancel₀ (D.sgn_ne_zero q.1), one_smul]
      rw [hkey]
      exact Submodule.smul_mem _ _ (mem_sIdeal_of_diag D wt hac)
    · rw [iPiece_eq_bot D wt h2] at hb; simp at hb; simp [hb]
  · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h1] at ha; simp at ha; simp [ha]

lemma sIdeal_mul_mem {a b : A} (ha : a ∈ sIdeal D wt) (hb : b ∈ sSub D wt) :
    a * b ∈ sIdeal D wt := by
  have hle : sIdeal D wt * sSub D wt ≤ sIdeal D wt := by
    unfold sIdeal sSub
    rw [Submodule.iSup_mul]
    refine iSup_le fun q => ?_
    rw [Submodule.mul_iSup]
    exact iSup_le fun q' => iPiece_mul_le D wt q q'
  exact hle (Submodule.mul_mem_mul ha hb)

lemma mul_sIdeal_mem {a b : A} (ha : a ∈ sSub D wt) (hb : b ∈ sIdeal D wt) :
    a * b ∈ sIdeal D wt := by
  have hle : sSub D wt * sIdeal D wt ≤ sIdeal D wt := by
    unfold sIdeal sSub
    rw [Submodule.iSup_mul]
    refine iSup_le fun q => ?_
    rw [Submodule.mul_iSup]
    exact iSup_le fun q' => mul_iPiece_le D wt q q'
  exact hle (Submodule.mul_mem_mul ha hb)

lemma d_sSub_le_sIdeal : Submodule.map D.d (sSub D wt) ≤ sIdeal D wt := by
  unfold sSub
  rw [Submodule.map_iSup]
  refine iSup_le fun q => ?_
  rintro x ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩
  rcases lt_trichotomy q.1 q.2 with h1 | h1 | h1
  · have hga : a ∈ 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) := by simpa [sPiece, h1] using ha
    have hda : D.d a ∈ 𝒜 (q.1 + 1, wt q.2) := by
      have := D.d_mem (q.1, wt q.2) a hga
      simpa using this
    rcases lt_or_eq_of_le (by omega : q.1 + 1 ≤ q.2) with h2 | h2
    · exact mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt h2 hda
    · refine mem_sIdeal_of_diag D wt (m := q.2) ?_
      simpa [show q.2 - 1 = q.1 from by omega] using hga
  · have hz : D.d a = 0 := by
      have hne : ¬ q.1 < q.2 := by omega
      simp only [sPiece, if_neg hne, if_pos h1] at ha
      simpa using ha.2
    simp [hz]
  · rw [sPiece_eq_bot D wt h1] at ha; simp at ha; simp [ha]

/-! ### Componentwise detection -/

lemma cmpL_mem_sPiece (hwt : 0 < wt 1) {a : A} (ha : a ∈ sSub D wt) (q : ℤ × ℤ) :
    cmpL 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) a ∈ sPiece D wt q := by
  induction ha using Submodule.iSup_induction' with
  | mem q' x hx =>
      by_cases hq : q' = q
      · subst hq
        rwa [cmpL_of_mem_same 𝒜 (sPiece_le_graded D wt q' hx)]
      · rw [cmpL_of_mem_ne 𝒜 (sPiece_le_graded D wt q' hx) ?_]
        · exact Submodule.zero_mem _
        · intro hcon
          simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at hcon
          exact hq (Prod.ext hcon.1 (wt_injective wt hwt hcon.2))
  | zero => simp
  | add x y _ _ hx hy => rw [map_add]; exact Submodule.add_mem _ hx hy

lemma cmpL_mem_iPiece (hwt : 0 < wt 1) {a : A} (ha : a ∈ sIdeal D wt) (q : ℤ × ℤ) :
    cmpL 𝒜 (q.1, wt q.2) a ∈ iPiece D wt q := by
  induction ha using Submodule.iSup_induction' with
  | mem q' x hx =>
      by_cases hq : q' = q
      · subst hq
        rwa [cmpL_of_mem_same 𝒜 (iPiece_le_graded D wt q' hx)]
      · rw [cmpL_of_mem_ne 𝒜 (iPiece_le_graded D wt q' hx) ?_]
        · exact Submodule.zero_mem _
        · intro hcon
          simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at hcon
          exact hq (Prod.ext hcon.1 (wt_injective wt hwt hcon.2))
  | zero => simp
  | add x y _ _ hx hy => rw [map_add]; exact Submodule.add_mem _ hx hy

lemma cmpL_eq_zero_of_notMem_range_sSub {a : A} (ha : a ∈ sSub D wt) {i : ℤ × ℤ}
    (hi : ∀ m : ℤ, i.2 ≠ wt m) : cmpL 𝒜 i a = 0 := by
  induction ha using Submodule.iSup_induction' with
  | mem q' x hx =>
      refine cmpL_of_mem_ne 𝒜 (sPiece_le_graded D wt q' hx) ?_
      intro hcon
      exact hi q'.2 (congrArg Prod.snd hcon).symm
  | zero => simp
  | add x y _ _ hx hy => rw [map_add, hx, hy, add_zero]

lemma cmpL_eq_zero_of_notMem_range_sIdeal {a : A} (ha : a ∈ sIdeal D wt) {i : ℤ × ℤ}
    (hi : ∀ m : ℤ, i.2 ≠ wt m) : cmpL 𝒜 i a = 0 :=
  cmpL_eq_zero_of_notMem_range_sSub D wt (sIdeal_le_sSub D wt ha) hi

/-! ### The main theorem -/

/-- **Purity implies formality, for any positive weight normalisation.**  If the cohomology of
the weight-graded dg-algebra `A` is concentrated on the line `w = wt n` (with `wt n = α n`,
`α > 0`), then `A` is formal: `A ⊇ sSub ↠ sSub / sIdeal` is a zig-zag of quasi-isomorphisms of
dg-algebras whose right-hand term carries the zero differential. -/
noncomputable def formality_of_pureFor (hwt : 0 < wt 1) (hpure : IsPureFor D wt) :
    StrictFormalityData D where
  sub := sSub D wt
  idl := sIdeal D wt
  one_mem := one_mem_sSub D wt
  mul_mem := fun _ ha _ hb => sSub_mul_mem D wt ha hb
  idl_le := sIdeal_le_sSub D wt
  mul_idl := fun _ ha _ hb => mul_sIdeal_mem D wt ha hb
  idl_mul := fun _ ha _ hb => sIdeal_mul_mem D wt ha hb
  d_sub := fun a ha => d_sSub_le_sIdeal D wt ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩
  qis_surj := by
    intro a ha
    classical
    set s := supp 𝒜 a with hs
    set P : ℤ × ℤ → Prop := fun i => ∃ m : ℤ, i.2 = wt m ∧ i.1 ≤ m with hP
    set z := ∑ i ∈ s.filter P, cmpL 𝒜 i a with hz
    have hsplit : a = z + ∑ i ∈ s.filter (fun i => ¬ P i), cmpL 𝒜 i a := by
      rw [hz, Finset.sum_filter_add_sum_filter_not]
      exact (sum_cmpL 𝒜 a).symm
    have hzsub : z ∈ sSub D wt := by
      refine Submodule.sum_mem _ fun i hi => ?_
      obtain ⟨m, hm, hle⟩ := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hi).2
      have hmem : cmpL 𝒜 i a ∈ 𝒜 (i.1, wt m) := by
        have := cmpL_mem 𝒜 a i
        rwa [show (i.1, wt m) = i from Prod.ext rfl hm.symm]
      rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hle with h | h
      · exact mem_sSub_of_lt D wt h hmem
      · subst h
        exact mem_sSub_of_diag D wt hmem (D.cmpL_cocycle ha i)
    have hzd : D.d z = 0 := by
      rw [hz, map_sum]
      exact Finset.sum_eq_zero fun i _ => D.cmpL_cocycle ha i
    obtain ⟨c, -, hc⟩ : ∃ c ∈ (⊤ : Submodule k A), D.d c
        = ∑ i ∈ s.filter (fun i => ¬ P i), cmpL 𝒜 i a := by
      refine exists_primitive_sum D fun i hi => ?_
      have hnp : ¬ P i := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hi).2
      have hne : i.2 ≠ wt i.1 := by
        intro hcon
        exact hnp ⟨i.1, hcon, le_rfl⟩
      obtain ⟨c, -, hc⟩ := hpure i.1 i.2 hne (cmpL 𝒜 i a)
        (by simpa using cmpL_mem 𝒜 a i) (D.cmpL_cocycle ha i)
      exact ⟨c, Submodule.mem_top, hc⟩
    exact ⟨z, hzsub, hzd, c, by rw [hc]; exact hsplit⟩
  qis_inj := by
    intro z hz c hc
    classical
    set s := supp 𝒜 c with hs
    set Q : ℤ × ℤ → Prop := fun i => ∃ m : ℤ, i.2 = wt m ∧ i.1 < m with hQ
    set c' := ∑ i ∈ s.filter Q, cmpL 𝒜 i c with hc'
    have hc'sub : c' ∈ sSub D wt := by
      refine Submodule.sum_mem _ fun i hi => ?_
      obtain ⟨m, hm, hlt⟩ := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hi).2
      refine mem_sSub_of_lt D wt hlt ?_
      have := cmpL_mem 𝒜 c i
      rwa [show (i.1, wt m) = i from Prod.ext rfl hm.symm]
    refine ⟨c', hc'sub, ?_⟩
    have hvanish : ∀ i ∈ s.filter (fun i => ¬ Q i), D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c) = 0 := by
      intro i hi
      have hnq : ¬ Q i := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hi).2
      have hcomp : cmpL 𝒜 (i.1 + 1, i.2) z = D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c) := by
        rw [hc]; exact D.cmpL_d c i.1 i.2
      have hzero : cmpL 𝒜 (i.1 + 1, i.2) z = 0 := by
        by_cases hex : ∃ m : ℤ, i.2 = wt m
        · obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hex
          have hge : m ≤ i.1 := by
            by_contra hlt
            exact hnq ⟨m, hm, by omega⟩
          have hmem := cmpL_mem_sPiece D wt hwt hz (i.1 + 1, m)
          have hb : sPiece D wt (i.1 + 1, m) = ⊥ :=
            sPiece_eq_bot D wt (by simpa using (by omega : m < i.1 + 1))
          rw [hb] at hmem
          have : cmpL 𝒜 (i.1 + 1, wt m) z = 0 := by simpa using hmem
          rwa [← hm] at this
        · push_neg at hex
          exact cmpL_eq_zero_of_notMem_range_sSub D wt hz (by simpa using hex)
      rw [← hcomp, hzero]
    calc z = D.d c := hc
      _ = ∑ i ∈ s, D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c) := by rw [← map_sum, sum_cmpL]
      _ = ∑ i ∈ s.filter Q, D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c)
            + ∑ i ∈ s.filter (fun i => ¬ Q i), D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c) :=
          (Finset.sum_filter_add_sum_filter_not _ _ _).symm
      _ = ∑ i ∈ s.filter Q, D.d (cmpL 𝒜 i c) := by
          rw [Finset.sum_eq_zero hvanish, add_zero]
      _ = D.d c' := by rw [hc', map_sum]
  idl_acyclic := by
    intro j hj hdj
    classical
    have key : ∀ i : ℤ × ℤ, ∃ c ∈ sIdeal D wt, D.d c = cmpL 𝒜 i j := by
      intro i
      by_cases hex : ∃ m : ℤ, i.2 = wt m
      · obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hex
        have hmem : cmpL 𝒜 (i.1, wt m) j ∈ iPiece D wt (i.1, m) :=
          cmpL_mem_iPiece D wt hwt hj (i.1, m)
        rw [show (i.1, wt m) = i from Prod.ext rfl hm.symm] at hmem
        rcases lt_trichotomy i.1 m with h1 | h1 | h1
        · have hne : i.2 ≠ wt i.1 := by
            rw [hm]
            exact fun hcon => absurd (wt_injective wt hwt hcon) (by omega)
          obtain ⟨c, hcmem, hc⟩ := hpure i.1 i.2 hne (cmpL 𝒜 i j)
            (by simpa using cmpL_mem 𝒜 j i) (D.cmpL_cocycle hdj i)
          refine ⟨c, mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (n := i.1 - 1) (m := m) (by omega) ?_, hc⟩
          rwa [← hm]
        · subst h1
          simp only [iPiece, lt_irrefl, if_false] at hmem
          obtain ⟨c, hcmem, hc⟩ := hmem
          exact ⟨c, mem_sIdeal_of_lt D wt (n := i.1 - 1) (m := i.1) (by omega) hcmem, hc⟩
        · have hb : iPiece D wt (i.1, m) = ⊥ :=
            iPiece_eq_bot D wt (by simpa using h1)
          rw [hb] at hmem
          have : cmpL 𝒜 i j = 0 := by simpa using hmem
          exact ⟨0, Submodule.zero_mem _, by simp [this]⟩
      · push_neg at hex
        have : cmpL 𝒜 i j = 0 :=
          cmpL_eq_zero_of_notMem_range_sIdeal D wt hj (by simpa using hex)
        exact ⟨0, Submodule.zero_mem _, by simp [this]⟩
    obtain ⟨c, hc, hdc⟩ := exists_primitive_sum (s := supp 𝒜 j) (f := fun i => cmpL 𝒜 i j)
      (P := sIdeal D wt) D (fun i _ => key i)
    exact ⟨c, hc, by rw [hdc, sum_cmpL]⟩

/-- Propositional form of the scaled main theorem. -/
theorem nonempty_strictFormalityData_of_pureFor (hwt : 0 < wt 1) (hpure : IsPureFor D wt) :
    Nonempty (StrictFormalityData D) :=
  ⟨formality_of_pureFor D wt hwt hpure⟩

/-- **Massey products vanish for any positive weight normalisation.**  For diagonal
bihomogeneous cocycles `x, y, z` of degrees `p, q, r` and weights `wt p, wt q, wt r`, purity
along the line `w = wt n` forces the triple Massey product to contain `0`.  The weight excess of
the Massey representative is `wt 1 > 0`, which is exactly what purity kills; for the degenerate
normalisation `wt = 0` the argument (and the conclusion) would fail. -/
theorem massey_zero_of_pureFor (hwt : 0 < wt 1) (hpure : IsPureFor D wt) {p q r : ℤ} {x y z : A}
    (hx : x ∈ 𝒜 (p, wt p)) (hy : y ∈ 𝒜 (q, wt q)) (hz : z ∈ 𝒜 (r, wt r))
    (hdx : D.d x = 0) (hdz : D.d z = 0)
    {u₀ v₀ : A} (hu₀ : D.d u₀ = x * y) (hv₀ : D.d v₀ = y * z) :
    ∃ u v c : A, D.d u = x * y ∧ D.d v = y * z ∧
      D.sgn p • (u * z) - x * v = D.d c := by
  have hxy : x * y ∈ 𝒜 (p + q, wt (p + q)) := by
    have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hx hy
    simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add] using this
  have hyz : y * z ∈ 𝒜 (q + r, wt (q + r)) := by
    have := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hy hz
    simpa [Prod.mk_add_mk, map_add] using this
  set u := cmpL 𝒜 (p + q - 1, wt (p + q)) u₀ with hu_def
  set v := cmpL 𝒜 (q + r - 1, wt (q + r)) v₀ with hv_def
  have hu_mem : u ∈ 𝒜 (p + q - 1, wt (p + q)) := cmpL_mem 𝒜 u₀ _
  have hv_mem : v ∈ 𝒜 (q + r - 1, wt (q + r)) := cmpL_mem 𝒜 v₀ _
  have hdu : D.d u = x * y := by
    have h := D.cmpL_d u₀ (p + q - 1) (wt (p + q))
    rw [show p + q - 1 + 1 = p + q from by ring] at h
    rw [hu_def, ← h, hu₀, cmpL_of_mem_same 𝒜 hxy]
  have hdv : D.d v = y * z := by
    have h := D.cmpL_d v₀ (q + r - 1) (wt (q + r))
    rw [show q + r - 1 + 1 = q + r from by ring] at h
    rw [hv_def, ← h, hv₀, cmpL_of_mem_same 𝒜 hyz]
  have huz : u * z ∈ 𝒜 (p + q + r - 1, wt (p + q + r)) := by
    have h := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hu_mem hz
    have he : ((p + q - 1 : ℤ), wt (p + q)) + ((r : ℤ), wt r)
        = ((p + q + r - 1 : ℤ), wt (p + q + r)) := by
      refine Prod.ext ?_ ?_
      · simp only [Prod.fst_add]; ring
      · simp only [Prod.snd_add, ← map_add]
    rwa [he] at h
  have hxv : x * v ∈ 𝒜 (p + q + r - 1, wt (p + q + r)) := by
    have h := SetLike.mul_mem_graded hx hv_mem
    have he : ((p : ℤ), wt p) + ((q + r - 1 : ℤ), wt (q + r))
        = ((p + q + r - 1 : ℤ), wt (p + q + r)) := by
      refine Prod.ext ?_ ?_
      · simp only [Prod.fst_add]; ring
      · simp only [Prod.snd_add, ← map_add]
        congr 1
        ring
    rwa [he] at h
  have hm_mem : D.sgn p • (u * z) - x * v ∈ 𝒜 (p + q + r - 1, wt (p + q + r)) :=
    Submodule.sub_mem _ (Submodule.smul_mem _ _ huz) hxv
  have hduz : D.d (u * z) = x * y * z := by
    rw [D.leibniz (p + q - 1) (wt (p + q)) u z hu_mem, hdu, hdz]
    simp
  have hdxv : D.d (x * v) = D.sgn p • (x * (y * z)) := by
    rw [D.leibniz p (wt p) x v hx, hdx, hdv]
    simp
  have hm_d : D.d (D.sgn p • (u * z) - x * v) = 0 := by
    rw [map_sub, map_smul, hduz, hdxv, mul_assoc, sub_self]
  have hne : wt (p + q + r) ≠ wt (p + q + r - 1) := by
    intro hcon
    have := wt_injective wt hwt hcon
    omega
  obtain ⟨c, -, hc⟩ := hpure (p + q + r - 1) (wt (p + q + r)) hne _ hm_mem hm_d
  exact ⟨u, v, c, hdu, hdv, hc.symm⟩

end WeightMonodromy

# Computational Evidence

Target statement: *a differential graded algebra with a compatible weight grading whose
cohomology is pure (weight = cohomological degree) is formal*, together with its Massey-product
consequences. This is the algebraic engine behind formality of the étale / de Rham cohomology
algebras of smooth proper rigid-analytic spaces satisfying the weight-monodromy conjecture.

The claim is a statement about arbitrary bigraded dg-algebras, so there is no sequence to look
up in the OEIS. What can be — and was — checked computationally is the *bookkeeping* of the
bidegrees, which is exactly where such a statement can silently fail. All arithmetic below is
elementary and was re-verified inside Lean as part of the proofs (the Lean files are the
authoritative artifact; nothing in this note is claimed as verified on its own).

## 1. Small-case bidegree table (the mechanism)

Write `(n, w)` for (cohomological degree, weight), `d : (n, w) → (n+1, w)`.
Purity means: cohomology only in bidegrees on the diagonal `w = n`.

| object | degree | weight | on diagonal? |
|---|---|---|---|
| cocycle `x` | `p` | `p` | yes |
| cocycle `y` | `q` | `q` | yes |
| cocycle `z` | `r` | `r` | yes |
| product `x·y` | `p+q` | `p+q` | yes |
| primitive `u`, `du = xy` | `p+q-1` | `p+q` | **no** (weight exceeds degree by 1) |
| Massey rep. `s·(u z) − x v` | `p+q+r-1` | `p+q+r` | **no** (excess 1) |

The single line that makes the theorem work: the excess `w − n` is additive under products and
is *raised by one* by every primitive that a Massey product needs. Purity annihilates every
class of nonzero excess, so every Massey product is forced to contain `0`.

Sanity checks of the same table for the degenerate cases:

* `p = q = r = 0` (degree-zero classes): Massey representative sits in bidegree `(-1, 0)`,
  still off-diagonal, still killed.
* if one rescales weights by `α` (`w = α·n`), the excess of the Massey representative is `α`;
  it vanishes precisely when `α = 0`. So the argument, and the theorem, are sharp exactly in the
  normalisations with `α ≠ 0`. This is the reason the formalisation fixes the standard
  normalisation `w = n` and records the general case as a future direction.

## 2. Truncation model: which pieces survive

For the strict formality zig-zag `A ⊇ A' ↠ A'/J` the pieces are

```
A'(n,w) = 𝒜(n,w)                       if n < w
        = cocycles in 𝒜(n,w)            if n = w
        = 0                             if n > w

J(n,w)  = 𝒜(n,w)                       if n < w
        = d(𝒜(n-1,w))                   if n = w
        = 0                             if n > w
```

Closure checks (all four cases were enumerated by hand before formalising, and each one appears
as a case split in the Lean proof of `pieceSub_mul_le` / `pieceIdeal_mul_le`):

| factors | degrees vs weights | product | in `A'`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| below × below | `n<w`, `m<v` | `n+m < w+v` | yes (below) |
| below × diagonal | `n<w`, `m=v` | `n+m < w+v` | yes (below) |
| diagonal × diagonal | `n=w`, `m=v` | `n+m = w+v`, both cocycles | yes (diagonal) |
| anything × above | piece is `0` | `0` | yes |

The only non-formal step is the diagonal × diagonal case, which needs the Leibniz rule; this is
what forces the Koszul-sign hypothesis to be nowhere zero.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

* **Is purity automatic?** No. `k[ℤ × ℤ]` with the tautological bigrading and zero differential
  has cohomology in every bidegree, in particular off the diagonal. Formalised and proved:
  `Examples.squareDGA_not_isWeightPure`.
* **Is purity vacuous?** No. `k[ℤ]` placed on the diagonal `n ↦ (n, n)` with zero differential
  is pure and has a nonzero, non-exact class in every degree. Formalised and proved:
  `Examples.diagonalDGA_isWeightPure`, `Examples.diagonalDGA_nontrivial_cohomology`.
* **Can a Massey product survive purity?** The bidegree table above says no, and the Lean proof
  `massey_zero_of_weightPure` confirms it. Conversely a genuinely nonvanishing Massey product
  forbids purity (`not_weightPure_of_massey`) — the algebraic shadow of the non-formal
  rigid-analytic surfaces.

No counterexample to any statement that was formalised was found; the two examples above were
found while probing the hypotheses and are now part of the formal development.

# Future Directions

Derived from the formal development in `Catalog/Novelty/WeightMonodromy*.lean`, which proves:
purity of a weight grading (weight `= α ·` degree, `α > 0`) on the cohomology of a bigraded
dg-algebra implies strict formality (`A ⊇ A' ↠ A'/J`, zero differential on the quotient), that
formality and purity each force triple Massey products to contain `0`, and that a genuinely
non-vanishing Massey product obstructs purity. Two explicit bigraded group-algebra examples show
the purity hypothesis is satisfiable and not automatic.

Each conjecture below is falsifiable, is stated so that it can be attacked directly in Lean on
top of the existing files, and is *not* implied by what is already proved.

---

## C1. Higher Massey products are killed by purity, with an exact excess formula

**Conjecture.** Let `A` be a weight-graded dg-algebra which is `wt`-pure with `wt 1 = α > 0`.
Then for every `n ≥ 3` and every defining system for an `n`-fold Massey product of diagonal
cocycles `x_1, …, x_n`, the resulting representative is a coboundary; more precisely, every
entry `a_{i,j}` of a bihomogeneous defining system has weight excess
`w − deg = α · (j − i)`, and the final representative has excess `α (n − 2) > 0`.

*The key insight is* that the weight excess is an additive "defect counter": products add it and
each primitive raises it by exactly `α`, so the excess of a Massey representative counts the
number of primitives used and can never return to `0`.

*Why now?* The `n = 3` case is fully formalised (`massey_zero_of_weightPure`,
`massey_zero_of_pureFor`) and its proof is exactly this excess count; what remains is the
combinatorics of defining systems and Koszul signs, which is now the only missing ingredient.
Falsifiable: exhibit a pure weight-graded dg-algebra with a nonzero 4-fold Massey product.

## C2. Purity is detected by the diagonal subalgebra alone

**Conjecture.** A weight-graded dg-algebra `A` is pure if and only if the inclusion of the
diagonal cocycle subalgebra `diagAlg ⊆ A` (already constructed, with zero differential) induces
a *surjection* on cohomology in every degree **and** the off-diagonal part of `A` is exact as a
complex in each fixed weight. In particular purity is equivalent to a statement about a single
strict subalgebra, with no reference to truncations.

*The key insight is* that `diagAlg → H(A)` is always multiplicative and its surjectivity is the
only place where purity was used in `diagonal_strict_section`; the converse direction should
recover weight-wise acyclicity from surjectivity plus a dimension/graded-Nakayama argument.

*Why now?* `diagSubalg_surjective_on_cohomology` supplies one direction verbatim; the converse
is a finite bookkeeping statement about the same objects. Falsifiable by an example where
`diagAlg` surjects on cohomology but some off-diagonal weight-complex has cohomology.

## C3. Non-formality of rigid-analytic surfaces has an explicit finite-dimensional witness

**Conjecture.** There is an explicit finite-dimensional bigraded dg-algebra over `Q` — of
Poincaré type of a surface, with `dim H^1 = 2`, `dim H^2 = 2` — carrying a triple Massey product
that is nonzero for *every* choice of primitives. By `not_weightPure_of_massey` such an algebra
admits no pure weight grading, giving a fully formal, self-contained counterpart of the
non-formal smooth proper rigid-analytic surfaces.

*The key insight is* that non-formality can be certified purely by a finite linear-algebra
computation (the Massey representative is not in the image of `d` restricted to one graded
piece), so the certificate is decidable once the multiplication table is fixed.

*Why now?* The obstruction theorem is proved; only the construction of one concrete bigraded
algebra instance (a `GradedAlgebra` structure on a finite-dimensional model) is missing, and
Mathlib's `AddMonoidAlgebra.gradeBy` machinery — used already in
`Catalog/Novelty/WeightMonodromyExamples.lean` — gives a template. Falsifiable: a proof that
every finite-dimensional bigraded model of a surface with these Betti numbers is formal.

## C4. Purity with `α = 0` fails: sharpness of the normalisation hypothesis

**Conjecture.** The hypothesis `0 < wt 1` in `formality_of_pureFor` cannot be dropped: there is
a weight-graded dg-algebra whose cohomology is concentrated in weight `0` in every degree
(i.e. `wt = 0`-pure) which is *not* formal, and indeed has a nonzero triple Massey product.

*The key insight is* that with `α = 0` the weight excess of a Massey representative is `0`, so
the weight count that drives every proof in this development degenerates precisely there — the
truncation `A'` also collapses, since the line `w = wt n` becomes horizontal.

*Why now?* Both proofs isolate the use of `α > 0` to a single inequality

for `α = 0`.

**Conjecture.** If `A` and `B` are weight-graded dg-algebras that are `wt`-pure, then the graded

Consequently formality for spaces satisfying weight-monodromy is stable under products and under

*The key insight is* that purity is a *pointwise* condition on bidegrees and the diagonal

*Why now?* The definitions in this development are already stated bidegree-wise, and the

# The Shape of a Space, Written in Weights

## When multiplication remembers more than addition

Take any reasonable space — a sphere, a torus, a surface carved out by polynomial equations — and you can attach to it a sequence of vector spaces, its cohomology groups $H^0, H^1, H^2, \dots$. Their dimensions are the classical Betti numbers: how many independent loops, how many independent voids. But cohomology carries more than a list of dimensions. Classes can be multiplied. The cup product turns $H^\bullet = \bigoplus_n H^n$ into a graded ring, and that ring already distinguishes spaces that the Betti numbers alone cannot tell apart.

Even the ring, though, is a shadow. It is the shadow cast by a much richer object: a *differential graded algebra*, or dga. A dga is an algebra $A$ with a grading by degree, a multiplication that adds degrees, and a differential $d$ raising degree by one, squaring to zero, and satisfying a signed Leibniz rule
$$d(ab) = (da)\,b + (-1)^{|a|}\, a\,(db).$$
Cocycles are elements with $da = 0$; coboundaries are elements of the form $dc$. The quotient $H(A) = \ker d / \operatorname{im} d$ is the cohomology algebra. Every space has such a model — the de Rham complex of differential forms is the archetype — and the model contains strictly more information than its cohomology.

How much more? That is the question of **formality**. A dga $A$ is called *formal* if it can be connected to its own cohomology algebra $H(A)$, endowed with the zero differential, by a chain of maps each of which is an isomorphism on cohomology. Formality says: nothing was lost. The cohomology ring is a complete invariant of the algebraic homotopy type of $A$; the multiplication table of $H(A)$ determines everything.

When a space fails to be formal, the failure is visible, and it is beautiful.

## Massey products: the ghost in the machine

Suppose $x, y, z$ are cocycles whose classes satisfy $[x][y] = 0$ and $[y][z] = 0$ in cohomology. Then the products themselves are coboundaries: there exist $u$ and $v$ with
$$du = xy, \qquad dv = yz.$$
Now form the element
$$m = \pm\, u z - x v .$$
A one-line computation with the Leibniz rule shows $dm = 0$: it is a cocycle, of degree $|x|+|y|+|z|-1$. Its class depends on the choices of $u$ and $v$, so what is well defined is a coset — the *triple Massey product* $\langle x, y, z\rangle$. The cohomology ring cannot see it; two spaces with identical cohomology rings can have different Massey products. And here is the crucial dichotomy:

> **Formality kills Massey products.** If a dga is formal, then every triple Massey product that is defined contains $0$.

So a nonzero Massey product is a certificate of non-formality — a ghost that survives the passage to cohomology and testifies that the ring was not the whole story. The classical example lives on a three-dimensional nilmanifold, modelled by the algebra generated by $x, y, z$ in degree $1$ with $dx = dy = 0$ and $dz = xy$. Then $[x][y] = 0$, $[y][y]=0$, and the Massey product $\langle x, y, y\rangle$ is represented by $zy$, which is closed but not exact. The space is not formal.

## Enter arithmetic: weights

Now change worlds. Instead of a smooth manifold, consider a smooth proper *rigid-analytic space* over a finite extension of the $p$-adic numbers $\mathbf{Q}_p$ — the $p$-adic analytic geometry that governs, among other things, the local structure of arithmetic varieties. Such spaces also have cohomology algebras: étale cohomology, de Rham cohomology. Are they formal?

The remarkable answer is: **yes, provided the space satisfies the weight-monodromy conjecture.**

What is a weight? In arithmetic geometry, cohomology groups come with a second grading, invisible in topology, produced by the action of Frobenius or by the monodromy filtration. Each cohomology class carries not only a *degree* $n$ but a *weight* $w$, and the multiplication respects both: weights add exactly as degrees do. Cohomology is therefore bigraded,
$$H^{n} = \bigoplus_{w} H^{n,w}.$$
The weight-monodromy conjecture of Deligne, in the $p$-adic setting, says that this bigrading is as tight as it could possibly be: the weight of a class of degree $n$ is exactly $n$. Everything sits on the diagonal $w = n$. This condition has a name of its own — **purity**.

Purity looks like a statement about arithmetic. It turns out to be a statement about homotopy theory in disguise, and the translation is the subject of this article.

## The main theorem: purity forces formality

Here is the algebraic engine, stated for its own sake and proved without any geometry.

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a $k$-algebra with a decomposition $A = \bigoplus_{(n,w) \in \mathbf{Z}^2} A^{n,w}$ into *bihomogeneous* pieces, with $A^{n,w} \cdot A^{n',w'} \subseteq A^{n+n', w+w'}$. Equip it with a $k$-linear differential $d$ that

* raises degree by one and **preserves weight**: $d(A^{n,w}) \subseteq A^{n+1,w}$;
* squares to zero: $d \circ d = 0$;
* obeys a Leibniz rule with an arbitrary nowhere-vanishing sign function $\varepsilon$: for $a \in A^{n,w}$ and any $b$,
$$d(ab) = (da)b + \varepsilon(n)\, a\,(db).$$

Call such data a **weight-graded dga**. (Allowing an arbitrary sign function rather than fixing $\varepsilon(n) = (-1)^n$ costs nothing and covers commutative, graded-commutative and sign-free conventions at once.)

Call the weight grading **pure** if, whenever $w \neq n$, every cocycle in $A^{n,w}$ is a coboundary — and moreover a coboundary of an element of the *same* weight $w$, necessarily in $A^{n-1,w}$. In words: all the cohomology sits on the diagonal.

> **Theorem (Purity implies formality).** A weight-graded dga whose weight grading is pure is formal. Explicitly, there is a subalgebra $A' \subseteq A$ closed under $d$, and a two-sided ideal $J \subseteq A'$ with $d(A') \subseteq J$, such that the zig-zag
> $$A \;\supseteq\; A' \;\twoheadrightarrow\; A'/J$$
> consists of maps inducing isomorphisms on cohomology, and $A'/J$ carries the **zero** differential. Hence $A'/J$ is the cohomology algebra of $A$, and $A$ is quasi-isomorphic to it.

The construction of $A'$ is the heart of the matter, and it is disarmingly simple: *truncate weight by weight*. Fix a weight $w$ and look at the subcomplex $A^{\bullet, w}$ — this is a genuine complex, because $d$ preserves weight. Keep

* everything in degrees $n < w$,
* only the cocycles in degree $n = w$,
* nothing in degrees $n > w$.

That is the canonical truncation $\tau_{\le w}$ of the weight-$w$ strand. Let $A'$ be the sum over all $w$ of these truncations. Let $J$ be the same thing with the diagonal contribution shrunk from cocycles to coboundaries: everything in degrees $n<w$, and in degree $n = w$ only the elements $dc$ with $c \in A^{w-1,w}$.

Two things must be checked, and both come down to the arithmetic of the inequality $n \le w$. First, that $A'$ is closed under multiplication and $J$ absorbs it: if $a$ lives at $(n,w)$ with $n \le w$ and $b$ at $(n',w')$ with $n' \le w'$, then $ab$ lives at $(n+n', w+w')$ and $n+n' \le w+w'$ — the region is closed under addition, and the boundary case $n = w$, $n'=w'$ is exactly where the Leibniz rule shows a product of cocycles is a cocycle. Second, that the two maps are quasi-isomorphisms. The inclusion $A' \subseteq A$ loses no cohomology: a cocycle of $A$ decomposes into bihomogeneous components, each of which is a cocycle; a component at $(n,w)$ with $n > w$ is off-diagonal, hence by purity a coboundary and thus invisible in cohomology, while all components with $n \le w$ already lie in $A'$. And the ideal $J$ is acyclic — a cocycle in $J$ is a coboundary of an element of $J$ — again because everything off the diagonal is exact, by purity.

The result is what one might call *strict* formality: not an abstract chain of quasi-isomorphisms through auxiliary objects, but two explicit maps, one an inclusion of a subalgebra, one a quotient by an ideal.

## A sharper picture: the diagonal subalgebra

Purity does something even more concrete. Consider the set of **diagonal cocycles**: elements that are bihomogeneous of bidegree $(n,n)$ — weight equal to degree, precisely the shape weight-monodromy predicts — and killed by $d$. Call the span of all of them $A^{\mathrm{diag}}$.

> **Theorem (Strict multiplicative lift).** $A^{\mathrm{diag}}$ is a subalgebra of $A$ containing $1$; the differential vanishes identically on it; and if the weight grading is pure, every cohomology class of $A$ has a representative in $A^{\mathrm{diag}}$. Consequently the cohomology algebra of $A$ is a quotient of the honest subalgebra $A^{\mathrm{diag}} \subseteq A$, on which $d$ is identically zero.

That it is a subalgebra follows because bidegrees $(n,n)$ and $(m,m)$ multiply to $(n+m, n+m)$, and products of cocycles are cocycles. That it hits every class is purity again: split a cocycle into bihomogeneous components, keep the diagonal ones, and observe that the off-diagonal components are all coboundaries — indeed a *single* coboundary, since a finite sum of coboundaries is one.

This is as strict as a formality statement can get. Ordinarily "the cohomology algebra is a subquotient with zero differential" is a wish; under purity it is literally true, with $A^{\mathrm{diag}}$ the subalgebra and its intersection with the coboundaries the ideal.

Making that last phrase precise requires knowing that cocycles multiply to cocycles and that coboundaries form a two-sided ideal among them: if $da = 0$ then $a\,dc$ is again a coboundary, and $(dc)\,b = d(cb)$ when $db = 0$. Both are consequences of the Leibniz rule — but note that the Leibniz rule is only available for *bihomogeneous* left factors, so both statements must be proved by decomposing into components and reassembling. That is exactly what the bigrading is for.

## The weight excess: why Massey products cannot survive

Now the two threads meet. Take diagonal cocycles $x, y, z$ of degrees $p, q, r$ — so of weights $p, q, r$ as well — with $xy$ and $yz$ exact. Choose primitives $u, v$ with $du = xy$, $dv = yz$, and take them bihomogeneous, which is legitimate because $d$ preserves bidegree up to the shift $(n,w) \mapsto (n+1,w)$. Then

* $xy$ has bidegree $(p+q, p+q)$, so $u$ has bidegree $(p+q-1,\, p+q)$;
* $yz$ has bidegree $(q+r, q+r)$, so $v$ has bidegree $(q+r-1,\, q+r)$.

Each primitive sits one step *off* the diagonal: its weight exceeds its degree by exactly one. Multiply back: the Massey representative $m = \varepsilon(p)\, uz - xv$ has degree $p+q+r-1$ but weight $p+q+r$. Its weight exceeds its degree by one. It is a cocycle. And purity says every off-diagonal cocycle is a coboundary.

> **Theorem (Purity kills triple Massey products).** In a pure weight-graded dga, if $x, y, z$ are diagonal cocycles with $xy$ and $yz$ exact, then there are primitives $u,v$ for which the Massey representative $\varepsilon(p)\,uz - xv$ is exact. Every triple Massey product of diagonal classes contains $0$.

Read the argument again and notice how little it uses: no spectral sequences, no obstruction theory, just a count. Define the **weight excess** of a bihomogeneous element as weight minus degree. Products add excess; taking a primitive raises excess by exactly one. Diagonal classes have excess $0$; each of the two primitives used in a triple Massey product contributes $+1$, and the two multiplications by diagonal classes contribute nothing — except that the representative has one degree fewer than the product of the three, so the net excess is $+1$. Purity annihilates anything with nonzero excess. The excess is a defect counter, and once it has been raised it can never come back down.

Turning the statement around gives the obstruction:

> **Theorem (Non-formality obstructs purity).** If a dga carries a genuinely non-vanishing triple Massey product of diagonal classes — no choice of primitives makes the representative exact — then no pure weight grading exists on it.

This is the algebraic shadow of the second half of the geometric story: there exist smooth proper rigid-analytic *surfaces* whose cohomology algebras are **not** formal. Their non-formality is detected by Massey products, and the theorem above says that such a space cannot carry the pure weight structure that weight-monodromy would supply. Formality is not a theorem about all rigid-analytic spaces; it is exactly a theorem about the ones weight-monodromy reaches.

## Twists, and why the normalisation does not matter

Arithmetic normalises weights in more than one way. A Tate twist doubles them; the interesting weight of $H^n$ is sometimes $2n$ rather than $n$; a comparison isomorphism may rescale everything by a fixed positive factor. It would be unpleasant if formality depended on a convention.

It does not. Fix any additive map $\mathrm{wt} : \mathbf{Z} \to \mathbf{Z}$ with $\mathrm{wt}(1) = \alpha > 0$, so $\mathrm{wt}(n) = \alpha n$, and call a weight-graded dga *pure along $\mathrm{wt}$* if there is no cohomology in bidegree $(n,w)$ unless $w = \alpha n$.

> **Theorem (Formality for arbitrary normalisations).** For any $\alpha > 0$, a weight-graded dga pure along $\mathrm{wt}(n) = \alpha n$ is formal, via the same strict zig-zag $A \supseteq A' \twoheadrightarrow A'/J$, where $A'$ is now the truncation along the line $w = \alpha n$. Triple Massey products of classes on that line again contain $0$. For $\alpha = 1$ this is the statement above.

One subtlety appears when $\alpha > 1$: the line $w = \alpha n$ misses most weights entirely. If $w$ is not a multiple of $\alpha$, the entire weight-$w$ subcomplex is acyclic and the truncation must discard it. The bookkeeping therefore indexes the pieces by pairs (degree, position along the line) rather than by bidegrees — a small change that makes the construction uniform in $\alpha$. The Massey argument survives verbatim, with the excess counted along the line: the representative has degree $p+q+r-1$ and weight $\alpha(p+q+r)$, and since $\alpha$ is positive, $\alpha(p+q+r) \neq \alpha(p+q+r-1)$, which is all that purity needs.

## Is purity a real hypothesis?

A conditional theorem is worth only as much as its hypothesis. Two examples settle the question, and they are as simple as one could hope.

For **consistency**, take the group algebra $k[\mathbf{Z}]$ — Laurent polynomials $k[X, X^{-1}]$ — bigraded by placing $X^n$ in bidegree $(n,n)$, with zero differential. This is a weight-graded dga; it is pure, because there is literally nothing off the diagonal to obstruct purity; and it is not degenerate, since in every degree $n$ the class of $X^n$ is a nonzero cohomology class which is not a coboundary. So the hypothesis of the formality theorem is satisfiable by objects with large cohomology algebras, not only by trivial ones.

For **independence**, take $k[\mathbf{Z}^2]$ bigraded tautologically — the basis element indexed by $(n,w)$ sits in bidegree $(n,w)$ — again with zero differential. Purity fails: the element indexed by $(0,1)$ is a nonzero cocycle in bidegree $(0,1)$, off the diagonal, and it is not a coboundary. So purity is a genuine restriction and not a theorem, and the conditional formality result is not secretly unconditional.

## What it means

Strip away the geometry and the theorem reads: *a second grading that pins the first one down forces all higher structure to collapse.* Formality is usually delicate, proved with hard analysis (Kähler identities and the $\partial\bar\partial$-lemma for compact Kähler manifolds) or with hard arithmetic (weights in the $\ell$-adic setting). What the argument above isolates is that the essential input is neither analysis nor arithmetic but a numerical coincidence: **degree equals weight, on the nose**. Once you have that, one canonical truncation and one addition of integers do the rest.

That is also why the counterexamples are so informative. A non-formal rigid-analytic surface is not merely a space where a proof technique fails; it is a space carrying a cohomology class — a Massey product — whose very existence is incompatible with the diagonal shape that weight-monodromy predicts. Formality and purity are two names for the same phenomenon, seen from homotopy theory and from arithmetic respectively, and Massey products are the currency in which the difference is measured.

Between the two lies a clean and testable statement, applying equally to $p$-adic geometry, to complex geometry with its Hodge weights, and to any other situation where a space's cohomology comes with a second grading that happens to line up with the first.
